checkpoints: Both choreography and orchestration implement the exact same core — a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating transaction standing in for rollback; the difference is only in who coordinates that chain, not what's being coordinated.

Choreography has no coordinator at all: each service subscribes to the shared event topic and decides for itself how to react, including running its own compensation when it hears the right failure event.
This makes it trivial to add a new service to the saga — just add one more consumer, with no coordinator to update.
But the saga's logic ends up scattered across every consumer, so nobody has a single place to see the whole flow or answer which step an order is currently stuck at.
Left unchecked this drifts into pub/sub spaghetti; the standard mitigation is stamping a correlation id (the orderId) onto every event so the timeline can be reconstructed from logs/tracing.

Orchestration answers that exact gap by introducing a coordinator — order-service itself acting as orchestrator, or a dedicated engine like Temporal or Step Functions — that explicitly commands each step and invokes compensation on failure, so the entire saga lives in one place that's easy to follow and easy to put a timeout on.

The cost is that the coordinator becomes a new central, stateful piece that has to track a state machine, retry safely, and survive its own crash, making it a potential single point of failure the system didn't have before.

The practical rule of thumb: a simple saga with few steps favors choreography's low ceremony, while a saga with many steps that needs oversight and timeouts favors orchestration's single source of truth.
One subject carries two completely independent design axes: delivery/fan-out and durability.

On the delivery axis, using different consumer groups (or plain subscribe) broadcasts a copy of the event to each group — use this when several independent businesses must each react to the same event (e.g. analytics, audit, and notification all listening on the same subject).

Multiple instances of the SAME consumer group (a queue group) instead load-share the event, each one handled by exactly one instance — use this to scale a single business horizontally without duplicate processing (e.g. three analytics replicas splitting the load).

On the durability axis, plain NATS core is fire-and-forget/at-most-once: a subscriber offline at emit time loses the event permanently, and emitting on a subject nobody is registered on drops silently with no error.
This fire-and-forget model trades reliability for very low latency and no storage/offset overhead.

When the business cannot tolerate loss (financial audit, payments), upgrade to JetStream/Kafka for a durable log, per-consumer offsets, replay of history, and at-least-once delivery, at the cost of higher latency and more operational complexity.
There is no universally best broker — the choice is made per use case along these two independent axes.

Kafka guarantees exactly one delivery per consumer group and splits a topic's partitions among the instances that belong to that group, so members of the same group divide the work between them rather than each receiving every message.
Different `groupId` values create independent consumer groups, and each independent group gets its own full copy of every event on the topic — that is what produces broadcast fan-out across services.

In this bootstrap config, inventory-service and notification-service are both started with `consumer: { groupId: "order-consumer" }`, so Kafka sees them as two instances of one group rather than two separate groups.

Because the two services share a group, the broker assigns the `order-events` topic's partitions between them and routes each event to whichever instance owns the partition it landed on, so a given order reaches only inventory or only notification, never both.

This explains the intermittent, seemingly random symptom: which service handles a given order depends on partition assignment, not on a dropped message or a broken handler — both `@EventPattern("order-events")` handlers are implemented correctly.

The fix is to give each service its own distinct `groupId` — `inventory-consumer` for inventory and `notification-consumer` for notification — so Kafka treats them as two independent groups and delivers a full copy of every `ORDER_CREATED` event to each.

The underlying rule is that different `groupId`s mean "everyone reacts" (broadcast), while the same `groupId` across multiple instances means "scale one role" (load-shared queue) — `groupId` is a routing decision, not a cosmetic label.

The fix can be verified by publishing one order and confirming both services now log/handle it, then adding a second replica of one service with the same `groupId` as its sibling and confirming events are still shared exactly-once within that group while the other service's group still gets its own full copy — showing that scaling one role neither duplicates handling nor breaks the other group's broadcast.

A handler that calls `repo.save(order)` and then separately calls `kafka.emit(...)` is a dual write: two independent operations against two different systems with nothing tying their outcomes together.

Once `repo.save` resolves, the order is durably committed to Postgres; if the process crashes or `kafka.emit` throws anywhere after that commit and before the publish succeeds, the event is gone forever while the order row stays saved — producing a silent, permanent divergence between the order database and Inventory.

Wrapping both calls in a single transaction cannot fix this, because a TypeORM/Postgres transaction only makes Postgres operations atomic with each other — it has no authority over a Kafka publish, and there is no two-phase-commit protocol spanning a database and a message broker here.
A try/catch with a retry around the Kafka call does not close the gap either, since a process crash before the retry executes still loses the event just as the unprotected call would.

The Transactional Outbox pattern fixes this by writing two rows — the `Order` and an `OutboxEvent` — inside the same database transaction, so either both commit or neither does, and `create()` itself no longer talks to Kafka at all.

A separate relay (a polling worker, or Change Data Capture such as Debezium tailing Postgres's write-ahead log) reads unprocessed rows from the outbox table and publishes them to Kafka, marking each row processed only after the publish succeeds, so a mid-flight crash just leaves the row to be picked up again on the next pass.

This redesign shifts the guarantee from possibly-lost to at-least-once: the event can no longer disappear, only arrive late or occasionally be delivered more than once, which means the Inventory consumer must dedupe (e.g. by `orderId`) to stay idempotent and avoid double-decrementing stock.

The fix can be verified by killing the process right after the outbox transaction commits but before the relay runs — the outbox row remains in Postgres, and the next relay pass (or Debezium) still eventually publishes it, closing the exact failure window the original code left open.

Protobuf serializes only the numeric field tag and its wire type onto the wire — never the field name — so the field name that appears in generated TypeScript is purely a local, cosmetic label with no bearing on what bytes are actually transmitted.

Renaming a field while keeping its tag number unchanged, such as `name` (tag 2) becoming `displayName` (tag 2), does not alter the transmitted bytes at all; it is fully backward-compatible, and every call site that references the old property name gets caught and rewritten by `tsc` itself.

Reassigning an already-released tag number to a different field, such as reusing tag 3 for `phone` after it meant `email`, is a wire-breaking change: during a rolling deploy, old and new binaries run side by side, so a message written by one version and read by the other decodes tag 3's bytes into the wrong field.

This kind of tag-reuse corruption fails silently — no exception is thrown and no crash occurs, because the wire type itself (length-delimited string, in this case) didn't change; only the semantic meaning attached to that tag did, so the bytes decode into a plausible-looking but wrong value.

A green `tsc` build is not evidence of wire safety here, because `tsc` only checks the generated TypeScript interface structurally against the current proto snapshot — it has no visibility into numeric wire tags and no knowledge of what tag numbers were already released and are running in production.

The correct fix for introducing a new field is to give it a brand-new, never-before-used tag number rather than repurposing a released one, and to mark any retired tag as `reserved` in the `.proto` file so it can never be accidentally claimed again.

Verifying this class of change requires more than local compilation: a cross-version wire test that encodes a message with the old generated type and decodes it with the new type (and vice versa) will surface the mismatch, and wiring a proto breaking-change linter such as `buf breaking` into CI catches released-tag reuse automatically before a human reviewer has to spot it.
Kafka models a topic as an immutable, append-only log.
A consumer does not delete a record on read — it only advances its group's offset (a position cursor) forward, while the data stays untouched in the log until the retention window closes.

This is the essential difference from a delete-on-ack queue like RabbitMQ or SQS, where the message vanishes permanently the instant one consumer finishes processing it and nobody can ever read it again.
Because the offset is state owned by each consumer group rather than stored on the message itself, many groups can read the same log fully independently with no effect on each other.

The direct consequence: a service added months later (analytics, audit) can just create a new consumer group and reset its offset to 0 to replay the entire retained history, with no producer resend required.
That replayability is the payoff of the log model — something a delete-after-consume queue never allows.
Kafka only guarantees FIFO ordering within a single partition — there is no such thing as whole-topic ordering, so the claim that pushing everything through Kafka guarantees ordering is wrong.

Each partition is an independent append-only log read sequentially by one consumer in the group; guaranteeing ordering across an entire topic would require partitions to synchronize with each other, killing the parallelism partitions exist to provide.

The one lever a developer actually has is the message key: the producer hashes the key with hash(key) % numPartitions to pick the target partition, so the same key always lands in the same partition and is processed in send order.

To keep ordering for one specific entity (e.g. every transaction of a single account), that entity's key (accountId) must be used for all of its events; leaving the key empty makes Kafka round-robin events across partitions, losing ordering immediately.

Choosing a narrower and tighter ordering scope is paid for with parallelism: the same key always routing to one partition means every event of that entity is handled sequentially by a single consumer, with no way to split that work across other consumers in the group.

Setting a dedup marker before the effect it represents has actually happened turns the marker into a claim about the future rather than a record of the past, so a crash between the claim and the effect leaves the marker orphaned with no matching state.

In this code, `redis.set(dedupKey, "1", "EX", 3600, "NX")` succeeds and returns before `repo.save(row)` is even attempted, so a process crash between those two lines leaves Redis believing the event was handled while Postgres has no row for it.

Because the Kafka offset was never committed when the crash happened, the broker redelivers the exact same message — and on redelivery `processEvent` finds the dedup key already set and throws `ConflictException`, silently discarding the only legitimate attempt to persist that event.

The happy-path tests (first-time processing succeeds, an exact duplicate gets skipped) never exercise a crash landing between the SETNX and the save, which is why the bug survives behind a fully green test suite.

The durable source of truth for "this event was processed" should be the effect itself — the Postgres row, ideally backed by a unique constraint on `clientMessageId` — rather than a cache entry that gets set ahead of that effect actually happening.

A correct restructuring persists the row first (or performs the dedup check and the write inside the same unit of work) and only writes or refreshes the Redis key after the database commit succeeds, turning Redis into a best-effort cache of an already-durable fact instead of a lock claimed in advance.

A smaller patch that doesn't change the ordering is to wrap the persist step in a try/catch and explicitly delete the dedup key on any failure that occurs after the SETNX, so a crash-and-retry sees a clean slate on the next redelivery instead of a stale orphaned key.

The fix can be verified by forcing `repo.save` to throw once, redelivering the same `clientMessageId`, and asserting the retry actually writes the row rather than being skipped as a duplicate, with exactly one row ending up in `processed_events` for that id.

Kafka's default partitioner hashes the message key to select a partition, so every event sharing the same key value always lands on the same partition, no matter how much total traffic the topic sees.

A partition key with low cardinality — such as `countryCode`, which only has around 15 distinct values — concentrates most events onto whichever partition the dominant value hashes to when real-world traffic is skewed toward one value, collapsing effective parallelism down to that single partition's consumer.

Kafka assigns at most one consumer per partition within a consumer group, so adding more consumers to an already-provisioned topic cannot reduce lag on one overloaded partition; the bottleneck is structural (key design), not a capacity shortage that more consumers would fix.

The correct fix is to change what the key represents rather than scale out consumers: re-keying on a high-cardinality, evenly-distributed field such as `orderId` or `accountId` spreads events roughly evenly across all partitions instead of piling onto one.

When ordering must genuinely be preserved for the scope currently baked into a low-cardinality key, a composite sub-key such as `countryCode#hashBucket(orderId, N)` keeps FIFO order within each bucket while spreading that key's overall volume across N partitions instead of one.

Sub-key sharding is a trade-off, not a free win: events are only guaranteed to stay in order within their bucket, not across the full original key's traffic, so the narrower ordering guarantee has to be an explicit, conscious choice rather than an assumed side effect.

Most real ordering invariants are per-entity (e.g. per-order or per-account) rather than per-broad-category (e.g. per-country), so re-scoping the partition key to the entity that actually needs ordering is usually both the correct guarantee and the higher-throughput choice.

Diagnosing and validating a hot-partition problem both rely on per-partition lag and offset data — via a tool like `kafka-consumer-groups --describe` or a lag dashboard — checked before and after a key change under comparably skewed load to confirm load actually redistributes evenly rather than just assuming the fix worked.

Sending every incoming message straight through a Postgres INSERT means the database performs a full write attempt, constraint check, and rollback for duplicates that never needed to touch a table at all -- this is what makes Postgres the throughput bottleneck as duplicate volume climbs.

Catching the unique(clientMessageId) violation (SQLSTATE 23505) is a correctness-preserving but expensive way to detect "already seen" -- the database only learns the write was unnecessary after already paying for the round-trip.

A fast atomic front layer such as Redis SETNX (`SET key "1" EX <ttl> NX`) answers "have I seen this clientMessageId?" in a single in-memory operation: the first arrival gets "OK" and proceeds to the DB write, while duplicates get null and are skipped before ever reaching Postgres.

The Postgres unique constraint must stay in place even after adding the Redis layer, because it remains the durable ground truth for cases the fast layer cannot cover -- TTL expiry or a Redis flush/restart that lets a duplicate slip past SETNX undetected.

Redis and Postgres trade off speed against durability: Redis is fast but lossy (bounded by TTL, wiped on flush or restart), Postgres is slow but authoritative, so neither layer alone gives both properties and both are needed together.

The TTL set on the dedup key is the tuning dial between the two properties -- a longer TTL keeps more duplicates cheap to reject at the cost of holding more memory for dedup keys, while a shorter TTL frees memory sooner but lets more duplicates fall through to the DB.
Reading the code is not enough to confirm the fix works -- it needs to be verified with a duplicate-storm benchmark comparing DB write count and consumer lag before and after adding the Redis layer.

A Redis-flush test proves the fallback actually functions: with the fast layer's state cleared, a duplicate should still be caught and rejected by the Postgres unique constraint, confirming the DB backstop is not merely decorative.
